chapter_title: Bharat Our Land (How I Taught My Grandmother to Read)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 6 periods = 300 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 5h 0min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading and Responding to the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.23): National Anthem table — states, mountain ranges, rivers.
Reflect and Respond (p.23): paired discussion on 'Jaya he' — meaning and significance.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud expressively, students follow in their textbooks. Ask students to listen for the refrain and any words that recur.
Students attempt the Reflect and Respond table (p.23), recalling states, mountain ranges, and rivers from the National Anthem. Teacher elicits responses and fills a shared table on the board.
In pairs, students discuss what 'Jaya he' conveys in the last two lines of the National Anthem, then share with the class. Teacher draws out ideas of victory, celebration, and collective pride.
Quick whole-class reflection: students identify one word from the poem that struck them and say why. Teacher closes by naming India's three-stanza structure as the frame the poem builds on.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem is translated from Tamil poet Subramania Bharati's verse, so students may be unfamiliar with the cultural allusions — brief context on Bharati enriches the read-aloud without slowing it. The parallel structure of each line in stanza one (treasure named, then peerlessness asserted) is the key formal feature students will return to throughout their reading of the poem. An unanchored task: word-meaning MCQ exercise at p.23 — direct students to attempt this independently as self-study.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for shared table

periods.activity_title: Summary, Mood, and Tone: Mapping the Poem's Features

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.25): fill-in summary using box words.
Check Your Understanding (p.25): mood, tone, rhyme scheme, personification.

homework.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.25): written response on impact of the refrain.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the poem's three-stanza movement — natural grandeur, human glory, philosophical depth — to orient the comprehension work.

Students complete the fill-in-the-blank summary using the box words at p.25 individually, then check in pairs. Teacher goes through answers, pausing on 'Brahma-knowledge' and 'Buddha's dhamma' to briefly explain the allusions.

Class works through the poem-features table at p.25: mood, tone, rhyme scheme, and personification. Teacher models the mood entry and invites students to build the remaining rows through whole-class discussion.
Teacher sets the homework question on the refrain's impact and gives a quick orientation: students should consider what changes — emotionally and rhythmically — each time the refrain returns.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem and discussed 'Jaya he' in the context of the National Anthem, students are ready to map the poem's formal features with guided support. A common difficulty at this stage is confusing mood (reader's feeling) with tone (poet's attitude) — it helps to ask 'How does reading this line make you feel?' versus 'How does the poet seem to feel about India?' Students who find the rhyme scheme column challenging can be directed to the refrain as an anchor line.

periods.activity_title: Devices at Work: Symbolism, Imagery, Hyphens, and Hyperbole

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.26): symbolism matching — Column 1 to Column 2.
Reading for Appreciation (p.26): hyphen impact — select all true statements.

homework.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.25): two examples of imagery from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Brief warm-up: teacher asks students to name two things India is compared to or represented by in the poem, drawing on their reading so far.
Students attempt the symbolism matching task at p.26 individually. Teacher then leads a whole-class discussion, asking students to justify each match by pointing to specific lines in the poem.

Teacher introduces the concept of hyperbole using the definition box, then students work on the true/false-style multiple-select question about hyphens at p.26. Class discusses why each statement is true or false, with teacher scribing agreed answers on the board.
Teacher sets homework on imagery examples and gives a quick scaffold: imagery appeals to the senses — sight, sound, touch, taste, smell — ask which senses the poem's descriptive language activates.

periods.teacher_notes: Having mapped the poem's mood, tone, and personification, students now engage with symbolism and the structural role of hyphens — the two most distinctive formal choices in the first stanza. A common pitfall is treating symbolism as simple comparison; the key is that each symbol (Himavant, Ganga, Upanishads) carries a cluster of cultural meanings that amplify the poem's patriotic argument. Unanchored tasks: hyperbole identification (p.26) and the ode identification task (p.26) — direct students to attempt these as self-study before the next encounter with the poem.

periods.activity_title: Allusion, Close Reading, and Suffix Word-Building

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.28): identify allusions — Upanishads, Brahma-knowledge, Buddha's dhamma.
Critical Reflection (p.28–29): extract-based close reading — five sub-questions on Himavant, Ganga, and Upanishads.
Vocabulary in Context (p.29): suffix table — find words from poem for -ous, -ity, -est, -less.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces allusion using the definition box at p.28, then students identify the three allusions (Upanishads, Brahma-knowledge, Buddha's dhamma) and discuss what each refers to. Teacher clarifies the philosophical weight each allusion carries in the poem's argument.
Students read the extract at p.28–29 and answer all five sub-questions individually. Teacher then leads a paired-exchange on the hardest sub-question: why the Ganga's movement is called graceful.

Students complete the suffix table at p.29, hunting through the poem for words ending in -ous, -ity, -est, and -less. Teacher builds a shared table on the board, inviting students to explain the meaning transformation each suffix creates.
Quick consolidation: teacher asks one student to name the allusion they found most powerful and explain why, linking it to the poem's patriotic purpose.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the poem's symbolic structure and hyphen effects, students now examine its deepest layer — the philosophical allusions that ground Bharati's claim for India's civilisational uniqueness. A common difficulty is distinguishing allusion from mere naming; the key is that each reference invokes a tradition larger than the words on the page. For the suffix task, students who struggle to find examples of -ity should be pointed to 'antiquity' in the third stanza.

periods.activity_title: Listening, Speaking About Place, and Descriptive Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.30): match pictures to speaker numbers — hiker, rock-climber.
Listen and Respond (p.31): match statements to speakers — two distractors included.
Speaking Activity (p.31): paired turns — praise assets of own village/town/city using cues.
Writing Task (p.31): paragraph on a memorable place visited — why, who, preparation, stay, activities.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the transcript (p.260) aloud twice. On the first listening, students match the two pictures to speaker numbers. On the second, they complete the statement-to-speaker matching task, noting that two statements are distractors.

Teacher leads a brief whole-class check on both listening tasks, asking students to name the detail in the transcript that confirmed each match. Distractors are discussed: why do they not fit any speaker?

In pairs, students take turns using the provided cues to speak about an asset of their village, town, or city. Teacher circulates, prompting students to give reasons for their praise and to respond to their partner's views.

Students write independently — a focused paragraph on a memorable place they have visited, covering the five prompts: why, who, preparation, stay, and activities. Teacher circulates and gives brief formative pointers on paragraph cohesion.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript features four speakers describing very different Indian landscapes — riverside, mountains, desert, and forest — which connects naturally to the poem's celebration of India's geographical diversity. A common difficulty in the matching task is confusing Speaker 2 (mountains, adventure sports) with Speaker 4 (forests, travel vlogging); direct students to the specific activity mentioned by each. For the writing task, students who write only in generalities should be prompted: 'name the place and one sensory detail that stayed with you.'

periods.activity_title: Synthesis: Extended Critical Reading, Suffix Sentences, and Beyond-Text Exploration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.29): five extended-answer questions — cultural identity, refrain, sages, warriors-music, national pride.
Vocabulary in Context (p.30): add new suffixes (-tion, -ive, -ment, -ed) and write sentences.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.31): find and share a patriotic poem or song in a regional language.

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.31): group interdisciplinary project on India's major geographical features.

time_bands.activity: Students work on the five extended-answer questions at p.29, drawing on the whole poem — cultural identity, the refrain's effect, sages, the warrior-music connection, and national pride. Teacher circulates and prompts students to cite specific lines as evidence for each answer.

Students complete the suffix table at p.30, generating new words with -tion, -ive, -ment, and -ed and writing an original sentence for each. Teacher draws out how word-building with suffixes extends the poem's vocabulary into their own writing.

Students share patriotic poems or songs from their regional languages — one or two volunteers share a title, a line, and its meaning. Class discusses how these texts echo or differ from Bharati's themes of India's natural and civilisational greatness.

Teacher introduces the group interdisciplinary project on India's geographical features as a homework task, clarifying the six categories (mountains, rivers, deserts, valleys, islands, plateaus) and the three required details per feature. Students form groups and note their assigned feature.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the poem's full argument — from its natural imagery through its human and philosophical claims — and asks students to articulate that argument in their own extended writing. Having explored allusion, symbolism, hyperbole, and the refrain across their reading of the poem, students are well positioned to connect specific devices to the poem's broader patriotic purpose. The multilingual exploration grounds the synthesis in students' lived linguistic experience, foregrounding the poem's own translated status as a bridge between Tamil and English.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for sharing regional poems/songs

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, symbolism, and cultural allusion using a patriotic ode as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Subramania Bharati's ode celebrating India's natural grandeur, spiritual heritage, and civilisational legacy.
items.item_stem:
Read the stanza on p.23 beginning “The mighty Himavant is ours-” and answer the questions below.
1. What does the word ‘mighty’ suggest about the Himavant, and which poetic device does this description exemplify?
2. The poet asks, ‘which other river can match her grace?’ rather than simply stating ‘no river matches the Ganga.’ What effect does this rhetorical question create for the reader?
items.visual_stimulus: Read the first stanza on p.23, beginning “The mighty Himavant is ours-”.

expected_elements: 1. 'Mighty' conveys immovable strength; device is hyperbole or imagery.
1. Accept symbolism (Himavant as emblem of national permanence).
2. Rhetorical question involves the reader, making the assertion feel self-evident.
2. Creates an elevated, chant-like tone that draws the reader into agreement.
Answers should reference specific words from the stanza.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, symbolism, and cultural allusion using a patriotic ode as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Subramania Bharati's ode celebrating India's natural grandeur, spiritual heritage, and civilisational legacy.
items.item_stem: The poem ends its first and third stanzas with the refrain ‘she’s peerless, let’s praise her!’ The pronoun ‘she’ personifies India throughout. Evaluate how the combination of personification and the recurring refrain works together to construct the poem’s patriotic argument. In your response, name at least two specific symbols from the poem — such as the Ganga, the Upanishads, or the Brahma-knowledge — and explain what each symbolises.

expected_elements: Identifies personification: India as 'she' — a mother-figure inspiring reverence.
Explains refrain as a structural device that builds cumulative emotional force.
Names and explains at least two symbols (e.g. Ganga = generosity and grace; Upanishads = unmatched scriptural wisdom).
Links devices to the poem's overall argument: India's greatness is self-evident, collective pride is a duty.
Evaluates effectiveness — does the combination persuade? Why or why not?

items.source_lo: Student matches spoken detail to visual and textual prompts by listening critically to multiple speakers using audio as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four speakers describing preferred Indian landscapes — riverside, mountains, desert, and forest.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the four speakers describing places they like to travel to (transcript on p.260). Then indicate whether each statement below is True or False, and give one word or phrase from the transcript that supports your verdict.
(1) Speaker 1 prefers an environment where she can reflect and find inner peace.
(2) Speaker 3 is drawn to landscapes that offer adventure and group activities.
(3) Speaker 4 explores biodiverse areas as part of his professional work.
(4) Speaker 2 has never visited the Western Ghats.

options.text: Speaker 1 prefers an environment where she can reflect and find inner peace.
Speaker 3 is drawn to landscapes that offer adventure and group activities.
Speaker 4 explores biodiverse areas as part of his professional work.
Speaker 2 has never visited the Western Ghats.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) True — supported by 'reflect, meditate, and find inner harmony.' (2) False — Speaker 3 is the photographer drawn to deserts, not adventure; Speaker 2 mentions adventure sports. (3) True — Speaker 4 describes himself as a travel vlogger exploring biodiverse areas. (4) False — Speaker 2 explicitly states 'A visit to the Western Ghats changed it all for me.'

items.source_lo: Student matches spoken detail to visual and textual prompts by listening critically to multiple speakers using audio as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four speakers describing preferred Indian landscapes — riverside, mountains, desert, and forest.
items.item_stem: After listening to the four speakers again (transcript on p.260), reflect on the following: Speaker 1 describes the riverside as a place for meditation; Speaker 3 calls the desert's beauty 'matchless.' In what ways do both speakers express something similar to the poet's feeling in 'Bharat Our Land,' and in what ways does each speaker's reason for loving the landscape differ from the other's? Give specific details from what you heard.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Both speakers echo the poem's reverence for India's natural landscapes — Speaker 1 finds spiritual peace in the riverside (like the poem's honouring of the Ganga), while Speaker 3 is drawn to the desert's visual beauty. They differ in motivation: Speaker 1 seeks inner harmony and reflection, while Speaker 3 is a photographer motivated by capturing unique images.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and justifies pride in a local place through structured paired oral exchange using prompted cues as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Paired praise of geographical, cultural, or historical assets of students' own village, town, or city.
items.item_stem: In one to two minutes, describe one feature — geographical, cultural, or historical — of your village, town, or city that you consider an asset. State what the feature is, why it matters to the people who live there, and use at least one vivid descriptive detail to help your listener picture it.

expected_elements: Names a specific feature (river, monument, tradition, festival, landscape).
Explains its significance to the local community with at least one reason.
Uses a vivid descriptive detail that appeals to the senses.
Speaks in organised turns — introduction, description, significance.
Maintains appropriate volume and clarity throughout.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and justifies pride in a local place through structured paired oral exchange using prompted cues as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Paired praise of geographical, cultural, or historical assets of students' own village, town, or city.
items.item_stem: A classmate has argued: 'Modern cities have lost their cultural identity — there is nothing truly special about where we live today.' Do you agree or disagree? In two to three minutes, argue your position with at least two reasons, using specific details about a place you know. Be prepared to respond to a follow-up question from the teacher.

expected_elements: States a clear agree or disagree position at the outset.
Gives at least two distinct reasons with specific local examples.
Acknowledges the opposing view before countering it.
Uses persuasive language to justify the stance with rationale.
Responds coherently when asked a follow-up question.

items.item_stem: Write a notice (80–100 words) for your school notice board inviting students to join a one-day trip to a heritage site or natural landmark near your town. Your notice must include: the name and location of the site, the date and time of departure and return, the purpose of the visit, and the name and contact detail of the teacher organising the trip.

expected_elements: Uses correct notice format: heading, school name, date, title.
Includes all four required details — site, date/time, purpose, contact.
Writes in formal, concise language appropriate for a school notice.
Stays within the 80–100 word range.
Names a real or plausible site connected to local heritage or geography.

items.source_lo: Student composes a descriptive personal paragraph on a remembered place, organising ideas across multiple prompts using independent writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A visit to a public heritage site sparking reflection on communal memory and local identity.
items.item_stem: Write a letter to the editor of your local newspaper (150–180 words) arguing that heritage sites and natural landmarks in your region deserve better maintenance and promotion. In your letter, name a specific site, describe what makes it significant, explain the threat or neglect it currently faces, and propose one concrete step that local authorities could take. Use formal letter-to-editor format.

expected_elements: Uses correct letter-to-editor format: sender address, date, editor's address, salutation, body, closing.
Names a specific site and explains its cultural or geographical significance.
Describes a real or plausible threat (neglect, lack of funds, pollution, encroachment).
Proposes one concrete, realistic step with a brief justification.
Maintains formal register throughout; argument is coherent and persuasive.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies suffixes to build new words and construct sentences using the poem's vocabulary as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Suffix patterns (-ous, -ity, -est, -less, -tion, -ive, -ment, -ed) drawn from the poem's own word stock.
items.item_stem:
The poem describes the Ganga as 'generous' and the land as 'sacred.' Using the suffixes -tion and -ment, transform the base words given below (which belong to the world of the poem) into new forms and write one original sentence for each transformed word that reflects a patriotic or geographical idea.
(a) Base word: celebrate → add -tion → new word: ___________ → your sentence: ___________
(b) Base word: enrich → add -ment → new word: ___________ → your sentence: ___________

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) celebration — e.g. 'The annual celebration of India's rivers brings communities together.' (b) enrichment — e.g. 'The enrichment of the land by the Ganga has supported civilisations for centuries.' Accept any grammatically correct sentence that uses the transformed word meaningfully.

items.source_lo: Student explores and shares patriotic expression across regional languages and investigates India's geographical heritage using multilingual exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Regional-language patriotic poems or songs shared alongside Bharati's translated Tamil ode.
items.item_stem: Choose a patriotic poem or song from any Indian language other than English — it may be in your mother tongue, a regional language you know, or a language you have researched. Write the title, the language it is in, and two to three sentences in English explaining what the poem or song praises about India or the poet's homeland. Then write one sentence saying how its theme is similar to or different from Subramania Bharati's 'Bharat Our Land.'

expected_elements: Names a specific poem or song with its title and language.
Explains in 2–3 sentences what the poem/song praises about India or the homeland.
Makes a clear comparison or contrast with Bharati's ode and its patriotic argument.
Shows understanding that 'Bharat Our Land' is itself a translation from Tamil.
Writing is coherent and uses appropriate vocabulary to describe cultural themes.

items.source_lo: Student explores and shares patriotic expression across regional languages and investigates India's geographical heritage using multilingual exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Regional-language patriotic poems or songs shared alongside Bharati's translated Tamil ode.
items.item_stem: In your group, prepare a short illustrated report (one A4 page) on ONE of India's geographical categories named in the poem — mountains, rivers, or a philosophical tradition (such as the Upanishads or the Buddha's dhamma). Your report must: name the specific feature, describe the region it belongs to, explain its importance in the lives of people living there, and mention one language spoken in that region. Include a hand-drawn sketch or diagram.

expected_elements: Names a specific geographical or cultural feature from the poem's world.
Describes the region accurately with at least one factual geographical detail.
Explains the feature's importance to the lives of local communities.
Names one language spoken in that region.
Includes a hand-drawn sketch or diagram that genuinely illustrates the feature.
